Laser beams are columnated light, unless there is something inside the building to disperse the beam and then something else to collect the "facially" reflected light this can't happen. There are wavelengths of light that can be created with a laser that can penetrate some building materials. But odd things happen. Wavelengths that can penetrate a lot of things have a long wavelength. The longer the wavelength the less resolution we have. Also these longer wavelengths start being absorbed by lots of things, typically metals---- which buildings have a lot of. Or water vapor in the case of THz radiation. It's funny, where you talk about the batman movie where they have all the cell phones essentially running sonar is way closer to reality then what you are describing. But two things. Sonar is a pressure wave hence the microphone and speaker. It also does not have good spatial resolution and probably fiendishly difficult to even get good room dimensionality with nevermind faces. Second, let's say you got smart and wanted to use bluetooth (2.4 GHz) which is a 12.5 cm wavelength, most faces look alike when your resolution is 12.5 cm. Going past the diffraction limit requires things (i.e. adaptive optics, apertures, different refractive index material etc.) that don't work on people's faces.

There is such a thing as remote generation of different wavelength radiation. Eg. starting with a visible light laser beam and turning it into THz radiation. But those beams are pretty strong and you need direct line of sight. Nevermind how fiendishly difficult it is to set up that sort of thing. The right google scholar term is 'remote THz generation" but it probably doesn't work the way you are thinking.

I think the other poster handled the microphone bit well enough so I will leave that be. But the laser recording vibrations from speaking, yeah that is easy. However to get really high signal to noise ratio, e.g. to hear someone from space (not likely possible) or something (more likely) via laser beam you have a a few problems. But the main one I suspect is how to have a really good filter. One trick we use for measuring really small signals is to modulate the frequency of the experiment. We choose a frequency far from other things if we can, e.g 60 Hz is bad because of the electricity, but so is 120 Hz as it is the 2x multiple. 10 Hz and below is bad due to road and building noise. Then you use a lock-in amplifier. Think of it as an adjustable notch filter that is tune-able to the wavelength your experiment is operating at. Big problem to me though is humans do not speak at one frequency.
